summary: Outlines architectural guidelines for developing Multipath TCP, which uses multiple paths at once for efficiency, resilience and throughput. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipath TCP lets one transport connection use several paths between hosts. RFC 6182 explains the design goals and architecture needed to preserve TCP's service to applications while working with existing network devices.

questions: how big should the mptcp receive buffer be
subtitle: Goals and architectural choices for extending TCP to use multiple network paths in one connection.

tldr.problem: A TCP connection normally uses one path even when hosts have multiple paths, limiting resilience and the use of available network capacity.
tldr.mechanism: MPTCP combines ordinary TCP subflows over different paths under a connection-level sequence space, while using TCP-compatible signaling and coupled congestion control.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6182 records goals and high-level design decisions for MPTCP, including compatibility with applications and middleboxes. It is Informational.

facts.label: Sequence spaces
facts.value: One connection-level and one per subflow

today: RFC 6182 is Informational and was published in March 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its security discussion points to RFC 6181.

sections.title: Why Use More Than One Path
sections.content:
Hosts may have multiple paths between them, but regular TCP uses one path for a connection. Multipath transport can use several paths at once to improve resilience when a path fails and make more network capacity available to end hosts.

MPTCP provides this service as a modified version of TCP and aims to remain transparent to existing applications. The RFC describes architectural principles and high-level decisions; companion documents specify protocol extensions, congestion control, and application considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: MPTCP can use multiple paths for one TCP connection. This can preserve connectivity when a path fails and use capacity on other paths.

sections.title: Performance and Compatibility Goals
sections.content:
MPTCP should provide throughput no worse than a regular TCP connection over the best available path and must be at least as resilient as single-path TCP. Hosts should negotiate its use automatically and fall back to regular TCP when the other host does not support it.

Applications should continue to receive TCP's reliable, in-order, byte-oriented service through a backward-compatible API. On the network, MPTCP aims to appear as TCP, traverse middleboxes, work across IPv4 and IPv6, and avoid taking more capacity at a shared bottleneck than a single TCP flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications should receive the same basic service as TCP, while the network should see TCP-compatible traffic. MPTCP must also avoid unfairly using bandwidth at shared bottlenecks.

sections.title: MPTCP and Its Subflows
sections.content:
MPTCP separates connection-level behavior from the TCP flows used on individual paths. The MPTCP layer preserves ordering and reliability for the application, while each subflow is an ordinary TCP flow that can be handled segment by segment by middleboxes.

The architecture has four functions: path management discovers and uses paths; packet scheduling assigns data to subflows and reorders it at the receiver; the subflow interface carries TCP traffic; and congestion control coordinates the subflows. A data sequence mapping relates subflow data to the connection-level byte stream.
sections.plainLanguage: MPTCP manages one connection made from TCP subflows on individual paths. It maps and reorders data so the application receives one ordered byte stream.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers, Reliability, and Signaling
sections.content:
MPTCP uses one sequence space for the connection and a separate sequence space for each subflow. The receiver uses a mapping between them to reassemble the application stream. This avoids sequence gaps within a subflow that could cause problems for middleboxes.

The design uses both subflow and connection-level acknowledgements. A segment must be retransmittable on another subflow if needed. MPTCP signals through TCP options, including an option on the SYN; if important control data is lost or stripped, the design can fall back to regular TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each subflow has its own sequence numbers, and the connection has a separate sequence space. A segment can be resent on a different subflow when a path fails.

sections.title: Buffers, Paths, and Security
sections.content:
The RFC recommends receive and send buffers of 2*sum(BW_i)*RTT_max, where RTT_max is the largest round-trip time across subflows. It notes that a fast path combined with a much slower path can require a large buffer, in which case the slow path may be better used only as backup.

MPTCP can use multiple address pairs to identify paths, and either host should be able to add subflows as paths appear or disappear. The security goals include checking that a new subflow belongs to the existing connection, verifying that a peer can receive traffic at a new address, and protecting requests against replay.
sections.plainLanguage: Buffer needs depend on the bandwidth and delay of the available paths. Before adding a path, MPTCP should verify that it belongs to the existing connection and can receive traffic.
